summary: Defines a Network Debugging Protocol to be used in an implementation of a PDP-11 network bootstrap device and a cross-network debugger.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 643 proposes a protocol for a remote host to debug processes on a PDP-11. It defines commands for controlling processes and reading or changing their state, plus replies that report success, failure or an unexpected stop.

questions: how did the network debugging protocol work
subtitle: A message protocol for a remote host to control and inspect PDP-11 processes.

tldr.problem: A remote debugger needed a way to request process-control and inspection actions from a PDP-11 over the network.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed level 2 protocol sends requests and replies on one link, with commands for stopping, resuming, examining and changing a process, managing breakpoints and reporting asynchronous stops.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies message fields and command behavior for a proposed debugging protocol and a subset for systems with fewer low-level debugging capabilities.

today: RFC 643 describes a proposed Network Debugging Protocol for PDP-11 processes and a remote debugger.

sections.title: A Network Debugging Protocol
sections.content:
The proposed protocol supports a PDP-11 network bootstrap service and a cross-network debugger. It assumes an operating system that can perform low-level debugging tasks such as setting breakpoints and single-stepping, though a subset could be used by a stand-alone program.

It operates at level 2 and bypasses the ARPANET Host-Host protocol. Requests and replies pass between the PDP-11 and remote debugger over one link, identified in the RFC as 377 octal.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote debugger sends requests directly to the PDP-11 and receives replies on one link. Some commands depend on the PDP-11 operating system supporting low-level debugging tasks.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
Each command contains an 8-bit op-code and process identifier, two 16-bit arguments and an optional string of 8-bit bytes. The op-code identifies the requested action; response codes indicate success, failure or an asynchronous process stop.

Commands include NOP to check whether the PDP-11 is operational; DEBUG and END DEBUG to claim or release control; STOP and RESUME; DEPOSIT and EXAMINE to write or read process memory; DEPOSIT STATE VECTOR; BREAK and UNBREAK; SINGLE STEP and PROCEED BPT; and process creation or destruction.
sections.plainLanguage: A command identifies an action and a process, with fields for its arguments and optional data. The PDP-11 replies with a success or failure code, or sends an asynchronous message when a process stops.

sections.title: Process Stops and State
sections.content:
When a process stops for a reason other than a remote STOP command, the PDP-11 sends an asynchronous reply with the process's state vector. The listed reasons include a trap, normal halt, breakpoint trap and trace trap after a single step. The state vector shown includes the registers, program counter and processor status.

DEBUG is refused if another remote host already controls the process or the process does not exist. Other commands can also fail when the remote host does not control that process or when the requested operation cannot be completed.
sections.plainLanguage: The PDP-11 reports when a process stops unexpectedly and includes its state vector. It refuses operations when the remote host does not have permission to debug that process.
